newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tax reform to boost competitiveness, jobs - Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: Tax reform to boost competitiveness, jobs - Rexrodt.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Thursday the coalition government's tax reform package would help boost his country's competitiveness in the global marketplace and boost job creation.
"Our concept for the tax reform is the most important answer to Germany's economic problems today -- globalisation, weak investment, unemployment and over-regulation," Rexrodt said in a statement.

A coalition tax working group chaired by Finance Minister Theo Waigel wrapped up a tax reform proposal which would slash income and corporate taxes while scrapping a slew of tax breaks in a bid to level the economic playing field.

The tax reform would reduce the burden on German taxpayers by a net 30 billion marks in two steps by 1999 -- although the cuts are not fully financed because no deal has yet been reached on raising value-added tax.
"The outstanding points of this reform concept are a big net tax reduction and a major cuts in tax rates," Rexrodt said.
Rexrodt added that reductions in profits on corporate taxes -- to begin next year -- would create conditions conducive to investment and decisively improve German competitiveness.

Under the plan, taxes on company profits would fall in two stages from their current 47 percent. Retained profits would be taxed in 1998 at 40 percent and profits paid to shareholders at 28 percent. The two rates would fall to 25 and 35 percent respectively in 1999.
"This concept above all marks an offensive by the government to create more jobs," Rexrodt said.
